title: Panic Room
full_review:
Tapping into fear, paranoia and protective instincts, director David Fincher traps his characters and the audience in a secret, claustrophobic hideaway in the involving thriller "Panic Room" (Columbia).

Still licking her wounds from a recent painful divorce, mousy Meg Altman (Jodie Foster) and her feisty teen-age daughter Sarah (Kristen Stewart) are spending their first night in their newly purchased, spacious New York City brownstone. In the first 10 minutes of the film, Fincher divulges all the pertinent information needed to set up the film's events. The brownstone was previously owned by an eccentric, paranoid millionaire who, wanting to keep safe from modern-day marauders (and greedy relatives) after his money, constructed a hidden room complete with a separate phone line, essential necessities like a fire blanket and water, and eight video monitors connected to cameras all over the home. It's a modern-day castle keep, or "panic room."

Just as mother and daughter float deeper into REM sleep, three robbers, Burnham (Forest Whitaker), Junior (Jared Leto) and the ski-masked Raoul (Dwight Yoakam), break in. It's up for grabs as to who is more surprised -- Meg and Sarah, awakening to find three men in their home, or the thieves, expecting to enter an empty house and instead finding a woman and child.

Forced to use a room they considered more a bizarre extra than a necessity, Meg and Sarah barricade themselves inside the tiny room, unaware that what the robbers want is inside with them: millions of dollars stashed away within the confines of the panic room's concrete walls. What ensues is a mental cat-and-mouse game as the characters try to outsmart each other to get what they want.

A few nifty twists in "Panic Room" and some splendid camera work add up to a better-than-average thriller. Just as the tension is built to white-knuckle height, Fincher breaks it with a sprinkling of spicy humor, only to resume the tense climb almost as soon as the laugh is finished. The script, written by David Koepp, gives the audience just enough information to understand and empathize with the characters while maintaining its focus on the suspense story. Burnham is the noble thief, wanting the money to build a better life for his child, and deploring any violence. Junior's motives are selfish, an attempt to amass more than he already has. Though Raoul's intentions are never clearly revealed, he is certainly the most vicious of the trio, brandishing a gun and plainly unafraid to use it, even with little provocation.

The film utilizes menace and fear more than outright violence, although when it does get around to it, the brutality is a bit fierce. But Fincher prefers to box in his characters -- and the audience with them -- as he ratchets up the nerve-racking pressure and suspense. However, a few things are left by the wayside in the process. It's hinted at that Meg suffers from claustrophobia, but she seems to control it exceedingly well. From the monitors in the panic room, Meg and Sarah can see the robbers' every move, but none of the three ever thinks to smash the cameras to bits, cutting off her visibility. (The fact that this obvious action is never done is partially explained with an amusing one-liner later in the film.)

Foster imbues timid Meg with an appealing vulnerability, making it all the more fun to watch her transformation into a protective Mama bear. Nicole Kidman was originally marked to play Meg, but Foster stepped in when Kidman was sidelined with a knee injury. The switch worked well. Whitaker emerges as the strongest of the robbing threesome, filling up the screen with his sorrowful eyes as his character wavers between doing what is right and taking what he needs. And although he is the hopeful thread in an otherwise desperate situation, Whitaker doesn't allow his character to be too sympathetic, which results in a more realistic characterization.

Though some of the contrivances are a bit preposterous, thanks to engaging portrayals and a brisk tempo, "Panic Room" holds the viewer's attention even when suspension of disbelief is necessary.

Due to some violence with much menace, fleeting drug use and recurring rough language with brief profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. (A-III) (R)
(
2002
)
